title: Quy Nhon food: 5 dishes to try

scenes.narration: Dish one, jumping shrimp pancakes. The name comes from the fresh little river shrimp, which jump as soon as they hit the hot mould. According to VnExpress, only My Cang, about twenty kilometres from the city, used to make them; now they are all over Quy Nhon. Rice batter with turmeric goes into small moulds, so each pancake is crispy and palm sized. To eat, roll it in rice paper with herbs and green mango, and dip it in garlic chili fish sauce. Try Anh Tu, Phuoc Son, or Ngoc Lien.

scenes.narration: Dish two, fish cake noodle soup, the classic Quy Nhon breakfast. A seaside city has fresh fish every morning, so the fish cakes are made on the spot. The fish is pounded by hand, then either fried golden or steamed, and the broth is simmered from fish bones and heads, so it is clear and lightly sweet. To eat, add fresh herbs, a little chili and lime, and sip the hot broth. Try Bun Thuy, run by three generations, Bun Ca Tuoi, or Van.

scenes.narration: Dish three, banh hoi with offal congee. According to VnExpress, banh hoi is a Binh Dinh specialty, and the best comes from Dieu Tri. Rice batter is pressed into very fine threads that weave into thin mats, topped with scallion oil. The congee is cooked thin from bone and pork offal broth. To eat, pick up the noodle mats with offal and herbs, dip them in chili fish sauce, then take a spoon of hot congee. Try ninety four Nguyen Hue, Thuy, or Co Huong.

scenes.narration: Dish four, banh can, which looks like the southern banh khot but comes from central Vietnam. Rice batter goes into clay moulds, covered over glowing charcoal, until the top is full of little holes and the bottom is golden. Fillings include egg, squid or shrimp. In Quy Nhon you can also eat them with a fish broth. To eat, dip them in sweet and sour garlic chili fish sauce, with fresh herbs. Try Co Du for the fish broth, or Co Nam for squid.

scenes.narration: Dish five, Cho Huyen nem. The craft of making nem is tied to Cho Huyen market in Phuoc Loc, Tuy Phuoc, and spread across Binh Dinh. Lean pork is pounded fine, wrapped in guava leaves and then banana leaves, and left to ferment for a few days until it turns sour. To eat, grill it over charcoal, or roll it in rice paper with herbs, star fruit and green banana, dipped in fish sauce with peanuts. Buy it at Moc Lan, Lam Qua, or Ong Bay.
